newsitem.title: UK: Britain to overhaul telephone codes yet again.
newsitem.headline: Britain to overhaul telephone codes yet again.

text.p: Telephone numbers in Britain are headed for their second controversial overhaul in 18 months with London dialling codes likely to be lengthened by a uniform 020 prefix next century, the industry watchdog said on Thursday.

Britain has barely recovered from the chaos of "PHONEday" in April 1995, when 27 million British telephone numbers were made redundant at a cost of 100 million pounds ($168 million) to telecoms giant British Telecommunications.

A spokesman for BT, Britain's main telecommunications player, said the latest proposed changes to dialling codes in London, Belfast (Northern Ireland), Cardiff (Wales), and the southern coastal cities of Southampton and Portsmouth could cost the group much more in network changes and information to help customers.

"We would accept that there is a need for more numbers in those areas," the spokesman said. "But we are concerned at the cost and the ongoing confusion. We are not certain that the plans have been thought through properly."

The opposition Labour Party scorned telecommunications regulator Oftel's latest plans as "a shambles", while small businesses bemoaned having to pay thousands of pounds to change stationary and logos on delivery vans and shopfronts.
In an bid to appease a storm of protests, an Oftel spokesman said a new London prefix would create a potential 64 million new telephone numbers, which should be enough for the time being.
"For the foreseeable future, we will only need another 13 million new numbers," he said.
Big businesses throughout the country may also see the prefix 05 added to telephone numbers.
However, final plans for new calling codes will only be announced next January.
Oftel had been considering using two prefixes for London -- 020 for inner London and 022 for outer London -- which could have yielded a 144 million new numbers.

But during a consultation period that ended last month, most businesses and consumer groups asked that the capital be given a single code. "We are taking those views on board," the Oftel spokesman said.
Oftel said it had "no idea" how much new codes would cost businesses and residents.
"The cost will be kept to a minimum by giving people as much warning as possible," the spokesman said, adding that most businesses only ordered office stationery on an annual basis.
London residents look set be given an 020 code, followed by the digit "7" if they live in central London or "8" if they live in the outer regions and their current telephone numbers.
Mobile phones and premium rate call numbers are also due for an overhaul.
